text: The interpretive history of the *bnei elohim* ("sons of God") in Genesis 6 is among the strangest in the reception of the Bible. The Book of Enoch, an ancient Jewish work preserved most fully in Ethiopic versions and read as scripture by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, elaborated a tradition of fallen angels, the Watchers, who descended to corrupt humanity in two ways: by forbidden teaching and by miscegenation. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 may presuppose this reading. Augustine, in *City of God*, rejected the angelic interpretation. He favored the Sethite genealogy instead, in which the sons of God are the godly line of Seth and the daughters of men are the line of Cain. Other readers have compared the passage with ancient Near Eastern traditions in which kings and other powerful men claimed descent from gods. The chapter also introduces the flood narrative, and that narrative belongs to a broader Mesopotamian tradition. Its fullest surviving forms are the *Atrahasis* epic and tablet XI of the *Epic of Gilgamesh* (the Utnapishtim narrative), both of which contain close parallels to the biblical flood story. The Hebrew word for the vessel Noah builds is *tevah* ("ark," "chest"). Outside the Noah story, Scripture uses *tevah* only for the basket in which the infant Moses is set adrift on the Nile.
